To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we propose a new discriminative pre-training task called ELECTRA, which is more sample-efficient than the masked language modeling task used by BERT; (2) ELECTRA learns contextual representations that substantially outperform those learned by BERT, given the same model architecture and training compute budget; (3) ELECTRA performs comparably to BERT and RoBERTa when trained on the same amount of data and using the same compute budget.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ELECTRA is a new approach for pre-training language representations that is more efficient than BERT, GPT, RoBERTa, and XLNet.
ELECTRA is more sample-efficient and more computationally efficient than other state-of-the-art models, and it can outperform them on various downstream tasks.
ELECTRA is a new pre-training approach for learning contextual representations of text.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

ELECTRA (pretraining text encoders as discriminators rather than generators) is more efficient than the current state-of-the-art pre-training methods, and the contextual representations learned are better.
ELECTRA is an efficient and effective approach for training language representations.
ELECTRA is an effective alternative to the current pre-training paradigm.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is often more effective to use a model as a discriminative classifier than as a generative model, even when the goal is to learn a generative model.
pre-training tasks based on predicting the identity of masked tokens are not the only effective way to pre-train text encoders.
discriminative pre-training tasks can be more sample-efficient than generative pre-training tasks, even though the former require more training examples to solve.
